newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Romatex sees no full recovery this year.
newsitem.headline: Romatex sees no full recovery this year.

text.p: Subdued South African consumer spending and illegal imports are likely to offset any trading benefits from a weaker rand, Romatex group managing director Michael Hankinson said on Thursday.

As a result, the textiles firm does not expect a full recovery in the year ahead after seeing net tax profits plummet to one million rand in the year to September 30, 1996 from 27 million rand the year before.
"While the weaker rand may aid our export drives, it is undermining the local economy and despite (some) positive trends, we do not expect a full recovery in the year ahead," Hankinson said.
In the firm's latest annual report Hankinson said that domestic markets had been "severely disrupted by the increased level of fraudulently imported goods.
"There has been a flood of substantially cheaper alternatives, which has forced local producers to reduce margins to remain price competitive," he said
The situation had been exacerbated by a surplus in global textile stocks, which had placed additional pressure on prices.
But steps by government and the Textile Federation industry body to stem the inflow of illegal imports appeared to be working and several tonnes of goods were presently impounded in state warehouses.
"The falling rand is also likely to play a role in curtailing these imports," Hankinson said.
While industry had accepted government's decision to phase down import tariffs, Romatex had been "disappointed by the slow reaction from government to introduce supply-side measures" in compensation.
In response to the move to introduce a free trade area in the Southern African Development Community by 2004, Romatex was determined to become more competitive and increase exports, he added.
